chunk_findings.detail: `_families` computes `single=f in HOT_SINGLES`, but `resolve` accepts a declared `Command` whose `family` is a hot-single name with a non-empty `action`. The generated `Family` is then marked `single=True` even though its `members` map contains both the hot single’s empty action and the extra action. For example, with `ddflow_identify` in `TOOLS` and a command `ddflow_extra` declared as `family="ddflow_identify", action="extra"`, `_families` returns `Family("ddflow_identify", {"": "ddflow_identify", "extra": "ddflow_extra"}, single=True)`. A caller that sees `single=True` omits the action enum, making `extra` unreachable and breaking the hot-single invariant, while no error is raised.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/families.py:135

chunk_findings.detail: The test passes `legacy={}`, so it never introduces a conflicting legacy mapping. A `resolve` implementation that prioritizes legacy entries whenever present would still pass this test because no legacy entry exists. The input `legacy={"ddflow_zed_go": ("ddflow_legacy", "old")}` is what would actually distinguish “declared wins” from “legacy wins”, and it is absent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_declared_families.py:test_a_declared_family_and_action_win_over_the_legacy_placement

chunk_findings.detail: `fam.members` is a dict, so `len(set(fam.members)) == len(fam.members)` is tautologically true: dict keys are unique by construction, and duplicate action keys would already have been collapsed by assignment. For example, a generated members dict that assigns `"record"` twice silently overwrites the first value, and this test still sees one key and passes, so it cannot catch duplicate action generation.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_declared_families.py:test_actions_are_unique_within_a_family

chunk_findings.detail: The test checks `F.HOT_SINGLES` against a separate hardcoded tuple and then checks counts, but it never verifies that the families with `single=True` are exactly `F.HOT_SINGLES`. Swapping the `single=True` flag between `ddflow_gate` and `ddflow_brief` keeps `len(fams) == 15`, `len(F.FAMILIES) == 24`, and the `F.HOT_SINGLES` tuple comparison passing, so the property named in the test is not actually asserted.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_declared_families.py:test_nine_hot_singles_and_fifteen_families_make_24_tools

chunk_findings.detail: Adding `family` and `action` in the middle of the `Command` dataclass, before `reason` and the served-by/value fields, changes the positional meaning of every later field. In any environment where `Command` is constructed positionally — e.g. `Command("run self", False, {}, "debug parity", "self")` — the pre-change values for `reason` and the served-by field now bind to `family` and `action`, leaving `reason` and the later parity fields empty. This silently corrupts MCP parity decisions. These new fields should be appended at the end of the dataclass or the dataclass should be made keyword-only, unless all existing positional callers are updated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/registry.py:590 (Command)

chunk_findings.detail: `resolve` does not reject every partially migrated `Command`. If a command has `action` set but `family` empty and its name exists in `_LEGACY`, the `elif family:` guard is false, so it falls through to `elif name in legacy:` and silently uses the legacy placement. For example, `DECLARED["ddflow_task_add"]` with `family=""` and `action="renamed"` returns legacy `Placement("ddflow_task", "add")` instead of raising. The declared `"renamed"` action is discarded, so `FAMILIES`/`ALIASES` can disagree with the declared matrix, violating the stated single-source rule.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/tools/families.py:resolve

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims a declared `Command.family`/`action` wins over the legacy placement, but it calls `F.resolve({"ddflow_zed_go": c}, legacy={})`. There is no conflicting legacy value, so the asserted precedence is never exercised. A `resolve` implementation that always prefers any non-empty legacy entry would still pass this test; it should pass something like `legacy={"ddflow_zed_go": ("ddflow_gate", "wrong")}`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_declared_families.py:test_a_declared_family_and_action_win_over_the_legacy_placement

chunk_findings.detail: The test checks that `F.HOT_SINGLES` equals the nine expected strings and that there are 15 non-single families, but it never checks that those nine hot-single names are present in `F.FAMILIES` (or `TOOLS`) as the `single` families. A faulty implementation could export the correct `HOT_SINGLES` tuple while omitting those tools from `F.FAMILIES` and `TOOLS`; all assertions in this file would still pass, leaving the required “9 hot singles” unverified.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_declared_families.py:test_nine_hot_singles_and_fifteen_families_make_24_tools

chunk_findings.detail: `fam.members` is used as a dict-like mapping elsewhere in this file (`fam.members.values()`, `fam.members[action]`), so `len(set(fam.members)) == len(fam.members)` is always true: mapping keys are already unique. Duplicate action declarations in the matrix would collapse when the dict is built, so this assertion cannot detect the uniqueness violation it is named for.

chunk_findings.detail: For a tool name already in `HOT_SINGLES`, `resolve` immediately places it as `Placement(name, "")` and `continue`s before reading that command’s `family`/`action`. So a declared command named `ddflow_identify` with `family="ddflow_identify", action="extra"` is accepted and the extra action is silently discarded, instead of being rejected as an invalid hot-single family declaration. This is the same hot-single-family invariant the previous finding targeted, but it is still unreachable for a hot-single tool’s own name; the declared matrix can contradict `HOT_SINGLES` and import does not fail.
